analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators permanently ban energy traders who manipulate electricity or gas markets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) a stronger stick against fraud in energy markets. Anyone caught manipulating electricity or natural gas prices, or filing false information about gas prices and availability, could be temporarily or permanently barred from buying or selling in those markets. It also makes it a specific violation to knowingly report false natural gas price data. It died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without ever being debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills. Manipulated prices and false market data push up the wholesale costs that flow into consumer bills; a ban from trading gives regulators a penalty that matters to repeat violators, beyond fines that firms can treat as a cost of doing business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households paying electricity and gas bills

how_it_helps.text: Lets FERC prohibit, temporarily or permanently, any person who manipulated electricity or natural gas markets from buying or selling energy, energy products like financial transmission rights, or transmission services.

Creates a new prohibition on willfully and knowingly filing false information about natural gas transportation, sales, prices, and availability with federal agencies or private price-reporting agencies, with intent to fraudulently affect the data.

Extends FERC's existing civil penalty and ban authority (Section 314 of the Federal Power Act and Section 20 of the Natural Gas Act) to cover these violations and to reach conduct done indirectly, not just by individuals acting alone.

analysis.who_pays: Energy traders, electricity marketers, and natural gas companies that manipulate prices or file false data would face the most serious consequence available short of criminal charges: being shut out of the market. Firms that trade clean pay nothing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy traders and gas sellers who cheat

drawbacks.text: FERC already has authority to impose civil penalties for manipulation; the bill's core addition is a trading ban. Critics of expanding FERC's enforcement powers have generally argued the commission's market-manipulation authority is broad enough, so the practical benefit beyond existing fines is hard to measure.

A permanent trading ban is a severe penalty decided by the regulator itself, and firms subject to it would argue it should require strict proof standards and judicial review to avoid being applied against legitimate trading strategies that look like manipulation after the fact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted enforcement upgrade: a trading ban and a false-reporting rule aimed at conduct that directly inflates energy costs for everyone else. The cost side is limited to the traders who would be caught cheating, plus a legitimate debate about how much proof a permanent ban should require. For ordinary ratepayers, the bill carries essentially no downside; its weakness is that it is modest relative to the size of the markets involved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2022, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 28, 2022, with Representatives Donald Beyer and Sean Casten as the other original sponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the committee never held a markup or reported it out.
The bill attracted 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill and any hope of a vote in that session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy traders and gas sellers are better off: with no law passed, manipulation of electricity and gas markets still carries only fines and penalties that already existed, with no risk of a permanent ban from the market, and no new prohibition on filing false price data.

sides.party_line_note: All three original sponsors were Democrats and its 2 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.industry: Electricity and natural gas traders and marketers
industries.note: Traders who manipulate energy prices or file false data could be banned from the market permanently, the strongest penalty available short of criminal law. Manipulated wholesale prices flow directly into household and business energy bills.

A new provision makes it a violation to willfully file false information about gas prices, availability, and transportation with federal or private price-reporting agencies. False data on gas prices is used to set contracts that consumers ultimately pay for.
